Dwie with a feminine noun, noun in the nominative plural: dwie kobiety.

Four is the last number that keeps the nominative: cztery domy.
From five upward the noun takes the genitive plural: pięć kotów.

items.why: Masculine nouns for people take -a. The other two are dative and instrumental.

A vehicle, but -u: samochodu. Memorise it.

Person → -a: przyjaciela. Plural is irregular: przyjaciół.

The -ę nouns expand: zwierzę → zwierzęcia. Plural: zwierząt.

-u, unlike komputer. This pair is worth memorising.

No ending, with a fleeting e: książek.

-i: miłości. Same form as the singular genitive.

Demonstrative and noun both genitive: tego pytania.
Both numeral and noun go genitive: dwóch kotów.

Trap: wbrew takes the dative plural: oczekiwaniom.

-ia → -ii when the i is its own syllable: Maria → Marii.

Clitic mi. It can never stand first in a sentence.

sets.title: Accusative singular
sets.ask: Which form is the accusative singular?

items.why: A person takes the genitive form: studenta. studentowi is the dative.
Animals are grammatically animate, so they take the same form as the genitive: kota.
The fleeting e drops out, exactly as in the genitive: pies → psa.
A soft stem gains -i- before the ending: koń → konia.
Person → genitive form → -a: lekarza. The rz stays hard.
Masculine nouns in -a decline like feminine ones: the accusative is -ę, not -a and not -y.
Same rule: kolega means a man, but it takes the feminine-style -ę.
A thing does not change: the accusative is identical to the nominative. stołu is the genitive.
No change. komputera is genitive — the form you need after nie mam.
No change. This is the pair learners get wrong most often: Mam samochód, but Nie mam samochodu.
No change. klucza belongs to the genitive: Szukam klucza.
No change, as with every masculine object.
Feminine -a → -ę. This is the ending to drill until it is automatic.
-a → -ę, and the k does not soften: książkę.
-a → -ę: kawę. kawy is the genitive — the form you need after nie lubię.
-a → -ę, and the c does not soften: ulicę.
Feminine nouns in a consonant do not change. noc is both nominative and accusative; nocą is instrumental.
No change: miłość is nominative and accusative alike.
No change. The case shows up only in the adjective: całą dłoń.
No change: Widzę mysz. myszy is genitive, dative and locative.
The exception to the -ę rule: pani takes -ą. Widzę panią.
Neuters never change in the accusative. okna is genitive.
No change, even with a soft stem: morze.
No change. A child is alive, but the animate rule applies only to masculine nouns — dziecko is neuter.
No change. The -ę is part of the stem, not an accusative ending.
No change: imię is nominative and accusative alike. imienia is genitive.

sets.title: Animate or not?
sets.ask: Which form belongs in the gap?

items.why: A thing does not change. samochodu is genitive — the form you need after a negation.
A male name is a person: Tomek → Tomka.
-a → -ę. kawy would be genitive, which you need after nie lubię.
No change. roweru is genitive: Nie mam roweru.
An animal is grammatically animate: kota.
Neuters never change. okna is genitive.
A female name in -a takes -ę: Annę.
A male name is a person: Piotra.
No change: mysz is nominative and accusative alike.
No change. Compare Szukam klucza — szukać demands the genitive.
A neuter does not change: drzewo.
No change. The animate rule is for masculine nouns only, whatever the meaning.
An animal takes the genitive form: konia.
Anioł is grammatically animate — a being that can act on its own — so it takes -a, though nobody has seen one.
A snowman is grammatically animate in Polish: bałwana. Grammar is not biology.
Robot behaves like an agent, so it takes the animate -a: robota.
Spirits and the undead are grammatically animate: ducha.
Male humans keep the genitive form in the plural: studentów.
Masculine personal → genitive plural, -y after a hardened stem: lekarzy.
Masculine personal, so the genitive plural applies even though the singular declined like a feminine: kolegów.
Irregular genitive plural with no ending: mężczyzn.
This is the trap. An animal is animate in the singular (psa) but NOT in the plural: psy, never psów.
Plural animals take the nominative form: koty. kotów belongs to the genitive — Nie ma kotów.
Things take the nominative plural: stoły.
The plural is the same as the nominative: klucze. No ending is added in the accusative.
Feminine plural is unchanged from the nominative: kobiety.
Unchanged: książki. (The genitive plural would be książek.)
Unchanged from the nominative plural: noce.
Unchanged from the nominative plural, which is irregular: dłonie.
Irregular plural, unchanged in the accusative: dzieci.

sets.ask: Which adjective form fills the gap?

items.why: The adjective follows the noun into the genitive form: nowego studenta.

Neuter adjectives do not change: nowe okno.

Animate masculine → genitive form: dużego psa.
A thing does not change, and neither does its adjective: duży dom.
A thing keeps the nominative shape: stary stół.
Feminine plural takes the nominative form: młode kobiety.

sets.ask: Which pronoun form fills the gap?

items.why: The accusative of ty is cię (unstressed) or ciebie (stressed). tobie is dative.

Masculine personal plural → tych, the same form as the genitive.
Cats are not masculine personal, so the pronoun does not change: te koty.
Animate masculine → genitive form: którego chłopca.
A thing keeps the nominative shape: mój dom.
Cats are not masculine personal, so the numeral keeps its nominative shape: dwa koty.

From five upwards the noun is genitive plural, and the numeral stays plain: pięć kotów.
For male humans the numeral changes as well: pięciu studentów.
Only masculine personal nouns change the numeral: trzy książki.
Feminine has its own form dwie, not the masculine-personal dwóch.

With an animate noun the numeral follows into the genitive form: jednego kota.
Numbers ending in 2–4 behave like 2–4, except 12–14: dwadzieścia dwa koty.

sets.ask: Which form does this verb demand?

Włączać takes the accusative, so a masculine thing stays unchanged: komputer.
Pilnować takes the genitive: Pilnuję dziecka.
Kochać takes the accusative, and a neuter does not change: dziecko.
Życzyć takes the genitive: Życzę ci szczęścia.

Zapominać takes the genitive: Zapomniałem klucza.

Bronić takes the genitive: Bronię prawdy.
Mówić takes the accusative: Mówię prawdę.
Szukać takes the genitive: Szukam pracy.
Lubić takes the accusative: Lubię pracę.
Czekać cannot take a bare object — it needs na plus the accusative: czekam na autobus.

sets.title: Negation flips it
sets.ask: What does the negation do to the object?

items.why: A negated verb turns the accusative object into the genitive: Nie mam czasu.
The affirmative used -ę; the negation needs the genitive -y: Nie lubię kawy.
Genitive plural: Nie mam pieniędzy. An extremely useful sentence.
Negation → genitive, even though the neuter showed no change in the affirmative.
Now the genitive plural does appear: Nie widzę kotów. The affirmative was Widzę koty.

items.q: Znam tę kobietę. → Nie znam ___ kobiety.
items.why: The pronoun follows into the genitive as well: Nie znam tej kobiety.

items.q: Lubię tę muzykę. → Nie lubię ___ muzyki.

items.why: Genitive: Nie piję mleka. Compare Nie ma mleka.

items.q: Idę na pocztę. → Nie idę na ___.
items.why: A negation only affects a direct object. After na the accusative stays: Nie idę na pocztę.

items.q: Mówię o tobie. → Nie mówię o ___.
items.why: After o the locative stays whatever the negation does: Nie mówię o tobie.
Nie ma always takes the genitive: Nie ma mleka.

sets.title: Prepositions
sets.ask: Which form does the preposition demand?

items.why: na meaning towards takes the accusative: na pocztę.
The same preposition with a location takes the locative: na poczcie.
Movement → accusative. A masculine thing does not change, so the form is stół.
Position → locative: na stole. This pair shows the whole distinction in one noun.
do always takes the genitive: do sklepu. Nothing to do with the accusative.
przez always takes the accusative, and a neuter does not change: przez okno.
Asking about something is o + accusative: pytam o film.
Talking about something is o + locative: mówię o filmie.
po meaning go and fetch takes the accusative: po chleb.
Games and sports take w + accusative: gram w piłkę.
wierzyć w takes the accusative, and Bóg is animate, so it takes the genitive shape: Boga.
za for a point in the future takes the accusative: za tydzień.

sets.title: Whole sentences
sets.ask: Type the missing word or phrase.

items.why: An animal takes the genitive form: kota.
A thing does not change, and the adjective agrees: nowy telefon.
-a → -ę: książkę. The adjective ciekawą already told you the case.
Names follow the nouns: Anna → Annę.
Animal → genitive form, with the fleeting e gone: psa.
No change. The genitive samochodu would be wrong here: ona ma samochód.
czekać needs na, and na here takes the accusative: na autobus.
Uczyć się governs the genitive: polskiego.
na towards a place takes the accusative: pocztę.
A bare accusative of duration. noc does not change; the adjective całą carries the case.
Singular, so the animate rule applies: studenta.
Plural male humans keep the genitive form: studentów.
za for future time takes the accusative: za tydzień.
Neuter takes -em, just like masculine: pióro → piórem.
Masculine -em: samochód → samochodem. And notice: no preposition for vehicles.
z + narzędnik; names in -a take -ą: Ania → Anią.
interesować się + narzędnik; feminine -ą: muzyka → muzyką.

być + profession → narzędnik: studentem. The plain form „Jest student" is the classic slip — in standard Polish the noun after „być" stands in the narzędnik. (The nominative has its own niches: see the Advanced corner.)
z (with) + narzędnik; after k write -iem: mleko → mlekiem.
Feminine -ą: lekarka → lekarką. („lekarkiem” would sound masculine.)
zostać + narzędnik; masculine words in -a take -ą: programista → programistą.
Masculine -em: kluczem. The tool needs no preposition in Polish.
bawić się + narzędnik; feminine -ą: piłka → piłką.
nad + narzędnik for a place where you stay: nad morzem.
Seasons as time words take narzędnik: latem, zimą, wiosną, jesienią.
The fixed phrase „moim zdaniem” — in my opinion.
ty → tobą in narzędnik. (ciebie is dopełniacz.)
ja → mną, and the preposition becomes ze before m: ze mną.
przyjaciele → przyjaciółmi — one of the -mi words.

items.q: Idę do pracy z ___. ((koleżanki — female friends))

sets.title: Under, over, with — which case?
sets.ask: Which case does the preposition need here?

items.q: The cat is sleeping under the table.
items.why: No movement → narzędnik: pod stołem. „Pod stół” would mean moving to under the table.

items.q: The cat ran under the table.
items.why: Movement → biernik: pod stół. This is the one place where these prepositions leave narzędnik.

items.q: We are sitting in front of the TV.
items.why: Static position → przed + narzędnik: przed telewizorem.

items.q: The park is behind the school.
items.why: za + narzędnik = behind (a place, no movement): za szkołą.

items.q: A lamp is hanging above the bed.
I am flying to the seaside.
items.why: Movement towards → nad + biernik: nad morze. „Nad morzem” = being there.

items.q: We spent the holidays at the seaside.
I will call you before dinner.
items.why: przed + narzędnik also for time: przed obiadem (before dinner).

items.q: Between us — I think Jan is right.
items.why: między + narzędnik: między nami; the phrase „między nami mówiąc” (= between us) is fixed like this.
opts: Między nami mówiąc, Jan ma rację.
Między nas mówiąc, Jan ma rację.
items.a: Między nami mówiąc, Jan ma rację.

sets.title: Type the form
sets.ask: Type the form the sentence needs.

items.q: To jest Ania. Idę do kina z [[Ania]].

items.why: oni → nimi (with the n- after a preposition).
The e drops out: pies → psem.

items.q: I am a student. ((a man speaking))
items.why: być + noun → narzędnik: studentem. The plain form „jestem student" is the classic slip; the nominative is only right in its own niches (presenting yourself, „to jest…", „jako…") — see the Advanced corner.

items.q: I am going for a walk with Anna.
I want to become a doctor. ((a man))
The keys are under the newspaper.
I drink milk with a straw.
items.hint: the thing you drink is NOT a tool
items.why: The straw is the tool → narzędnik (słomką). The milk is what you drink → biernik (mleko). Two narzędniks in a row — „piję mlekiem słomką" — would leave the sentence without an object.
items.display: Piję mleko słomką. / Piję mleko przez słomkę.

items.why: Means of transport → bare narzędnik: tramwajem.
Here z means „from” → dopełniacz: z pracy. With „with” it would be narzędnik: z pracą (e.g. mam problem z pracą).

items.q: Choose the correct sentence: „I play the guitar.”
items.why: grać + na + miejscownik — even though a guitar feels like a tool.
Adjective and noun both in narzędnik: dobrą koleżanką.
bać się takes dopełniacz (psa) — unlike interessować się (+ narzędnik). The classic mix-up.
ja → mną; the preposition becomes ze before m.
zostać + narzędnik; for a woman use the feminine lekarką.

items.q: Choose the standard way to say „I am tired.”
items.why: być + adjective keeps the plain form: Jestem zmęczony. The -ym shape appears after verbs like wydawać się / okazywać się.
Seasons as time words: zimą, latem, wiosną, jesienią.
Static position → przed + narzędnik: przed domem.
Both words in narzędnik: nowymi uczniami (uczeń → uczniowie → uczniami).
Tool → bare narzędnik; e drops: ołówek → ołówkiem.

sets.title: Which ending?
sets.ask: Which is the correct locative singular?

items.why: k, g, ch and l take -u in masculine nouns: w banku. (bankowi is dative, bankiem instrumental.)
l takes -u in masculine and neuter: w hotelu. In feminine nouns l takes -i instead: sól → soli.
Hard stem takes -e, and -e softens: st → ść and a → e together. w mieście.
s takes -e, with the vowel shift a → e: w lesie.
ł becomes l before -e: na stole. It takes -e even though it looks like an -l stem, because that l is a softened ł.
c is hardened, so feminine nouns take -y, not -i: w pracy. This is the trap that catches almost everyone.
In feminine nouns l behaves as soft and takes -i: o soli. Compare masculine hotel → hotelu.
ż is hardened, so -y: na plaży.
A soft stem takes -u: o koniu. No softening is needed because the stem is already soft.
Hardened cz takes -u in masculine nouns: o graczu. Feminine hardened stems take -y instead — the genders differ.
A soft stem takes -u: w morzu.
k takes -u: o dziecku. The plural is irregular: o dzieciach.
A hard stem other than k, g, ch, l takes -e: w sklepie.
Every regular plural takes -ach: w lasach.
n softens to ni before -e: w kinie.
r softens to rz before -e: o biurze.
n softens to ni: w Lublinie.
-ów becomes -ow- and w behaves as soft: w Krakowie.
A soft stem takes -u, and the spelling n + i keeps it soft: w Poznaniu.
w behaves as soft, so -u is spelled -iu: we Wrocławiu.
One of exactly three countries that take -ech instead of -ach: w Niemczech.
The second of the three: we Włoszech. Note the preposition becomes we before the W- cluster.
The third of the three: na Węgrzech.

items.hint: looks like an exception — it is not
items.why: Czechy is completely regular: w Czechach. Only Niemcy, Włochy and Węgry take -ech.
Regular -ach: w Chinach. Compare the trap: Niemcy → Niemczech.
A plural-only noun: w drzwiach (in the doorway).
Regular -ach: w wakacjach. For 'on holiday' Polish prefers na wakacjach.
ludzie → o ludziach. The stem looks irregular, but the plural ending is the ordinary -ach.
o dzieciach. Note that dziecko → o dziecku in the singular but o dzieciach in the plural.
we (not w) before a W followed by a consonant: we Włoszech, we Francji, we Wrocławiu.
The cluster fr- takes we: we Francji. When the cluster cannot be pronounced without it, Polish inserts e.
k → c, and the preposition stays w because Polska does not begin with a consonant cluster: w Polsce.
Neuter singular takes -ym after a hard stem: w dużym mieście.
Every feminine singular adjective takes -ej: w nowej szkole.
The plural takes -ych after a hard stem: o dobrych ludziach.
Soft stems take -im: o tanim człowieku.
After k Polish writes -im: w polskim kraju.
ten → tym (m/n), tej (f), tych (pl): o tej sprawie.
który behaves like a hard-stem adjective: o którym dniu.
mój → moim / mojej / moich: o mojej książce.
nasz behaves like a hard-stem adjective: w naszym domu.
swój → swoim / swojej / swoich: w swoim mieszkaniu.
Numerals take -u, here spelled -ech on the soft stem: o trzech osobach.
The collective numerals take -gu: o dwojgu dzieciach.
dwa has two accepted locative forms, dwu and dwóch: o dwóch ludziach.
ja → mnie in the locative: mówią o mnie.
After a preposition the third person takes n-: o nim. (go is genitive/accusative, jemu is dative.)
o niej. The n- appears because a preposition stands in front; jej is the form without n-.
my → nas in the locative: mówią o nas. (nami is the instrumental, nam the dative.)
The reflexive locative is sobie: myśli tylko o sobie.

sets.title: Which preposition?
sets.ask: Choose the preposition the verb needs.

items.why: mówić / rozmawiać o + locative: rozmawiamy o pracy.
polegać na + locative — never w: polegam na tobie.
upierać się przy + locative: upieram się przy swoim zdaniu.
po + locative for movement around or over an area: spacerujemy po parku.
w + locative for being inside: mieszkam w Krakowie.
na + locative for events and open spaces: jestem na koncercie.
przy + locative means beside, at: siedzę przy stole.
myśleć o + locative: myślę o tobie.
znać się na + locative. Plain znać takes the accusative: znam ten komputer.
koncentrować się na + locative: koncentruję się na zadaniu.
pracować przy + locative when you mean at the machine: pracuję przy komputerze. pracować w + locative means to work in a place: pracuję w biurze.
zapomnieć o + locative: zapomniałem o spotkaniu.
opowiadać o + locative: opowiadam o wakacjach.
zależeć na + locative: zależy mi na tobie.
szukać po + locative: szukać po kątach.
w domu = at home. Note that dom takes -u despite a hard stem.
na wakacjach is the idiomatic phrase.

sets.title: Place or movement?
sets.ask: Choose the right preposition — and watch the case.

items.q: Kot śpi ___ stołem. ((under the table — no movement))
items.why: Static position with pod takes the instrumental, not the locative: kot śpi pod stołem. This item tests the preposition; the case follows from the verb.
przed + instrumental for a static position: przed telewizorem. With movement it would take the accusative: stanął przed telewizor.
za + instrumental = behind (static): park jest za szkołą. za + accusative = to behind (movement).
nad + instrumental for a static position: nad łóżkiem wisi lampa.
A warning, not a locative example: movement towards takes the accusative — lecę nad morze. Staying there is nad morzem.
Static, so the instrumental: nad morzem. Movement towards would give nad morze with the accusative.
przed + instrumental also covers time: przed obiadem.
po + locative for time after: po obiedzie.
w + locative for cities: w Warszawie.
Regions and islands take na: na Śląsku, na Mazowszu, na Podhalu, na Węgrzech, na Kubie.
na Słowacji is the standard form. (For Ukraine both na Ukrainie and w Ukrainie are correct — the Rada Języka Polskiego accepts both since 2022.)
na uniwersytecie — universities, like many institutions and events, take na.
w drzwiach = in the doorway. drzwi is plural-only: w drzwiach.
o + locative with the reflexive sobie: myśli tylko o sobie.
w + locative for Poland: w Polsce. Countries normally take w; the plural exceptions are Niemcy, Włochy and Węgry, and a few countries take na (Ukraina, Słowacja, Węgry).
st → ść and a → e: w mieście.
s takes -e with a → e: w lesie.
In feminine nouns l takes -i: o soli.
Hardened cz takes -u in the masculine: o graczu.
l takes -u in the masculine: w hotelu.
w behaves as soft: w Warszawie.
One of the three -ech countries: w Niemczech.

items.hint: regular, despite looking like the others

items.why: The plural is regular -ach: o dzieciach.
oko → w oku. The plural is irregular: w oczach.
ucho → w uchu. The plural is irregular: w uszach.

items.hint: imię — neuter, and a fixed phrase
items.why: imię → w imieniu. The phrase w imieniu means on behalf of.
-um nouns keep -um in the singular: w muzeum.
w centrum — unchanged in the singular.
wieś → wsi. The final ś becomes si.
s → ś and ł → l: w Wiśle.
n → ni: w Ukrainie. The older na Ukrainie is also correct.
Hardened rz takes -y in the feminine: w twarzy.
k → c: w ręce. The form w ręku is also correct — PWN accepts both.
The singular is regular: o przyjacielu. The plural stem is different: o przyjaciołach.
The plural uses the stem przyjaciol-: o przyjaciołach.
tydzień → tygodniu, and the plural is o tygodniach.

items.q: I live in a small town.
items.why: w + locative, and the adjective agrees: w małym miasteczku.
znać się na + locative: na komputerach.

items.q: We are walking around the park.
I am sitting at the table.

items.why: w Niemczech — one of the three -ech countries.

items.q: I have never been to Italy.
items.why: we Włoszech — note both the irregular ending and the we.

items.q: The book is on the table.
items.why: na + locative for a static position: na stole.

items.q: I am focusing on the task.

items.why: The reflexive locative is sobie: o sobie.

items.q: In the evening I read books.
items.why: wieczorem ('in the evening') is an instrumental time expression with no preposition — a useful contrast with w + locative.
na wsi = in the countryside. wieś → wsi.
Hardened c takes -y in the feminine: w pracy.
Hardened cz takes -u in the masculine: o graczu. The plural is o graczach.
Hard-stem plural takes -ych: o dobrych ludziach.
After k write -im: w polskim kraju.
Hard t softens to ci before -e: kot → kocie. Same shape as the locative, o kocie.
The fleeting e drops and s stays hard: pies → psie. Compare the genitive psa.
n → ni before -e: pan → panie. Panu is the dative.
ł becomes l and takes -e: stół → stole. The ó returns to o.
k takes -u and the e drops: Marek → Marku. Never Mareku.
Hardened sz takes -u with no softening: Tomasz → Tomaszu.
l is functionally soft, so it takes -u: król → królu. Compare Michał → Michale, where ł → l plus -e.
cz → -u: klucz → kluczu. Klucze is the plural.
Soft ń → -u and the e drops: uczeń → uczniu.
One of the four exceptions: chłopiec → chłopcze, with c → cz. Chłopcu does not exist.
Another of the four: ojciec → ojcze. Ojcu would be the locative of a different pattern, and is wrong here.
Bóg → Boże, the relic -e form. Bogu is dative and locative, never the vocative.
ksiądz → księże: the nasal ą becomes ę and dz becomes ż. Księdzu is the locative.
syn → synu, the relic of the old u-stems. It happens to match the locative, o synu.
k → -u: człowieku. The poetic człowiecze belongs to old literature.
An inanimate -ec noun: the neutral form is palcu. Palcze is not used.
taniec → tańcu, with ń before c. The -e variant would be elevated, and is not used for dancing.
d → dzi and ó → o: samochód → samochodzie.
d → dzi with the vowel change ą → ę: sąsiad → sąsiedzie.
Every feminine in -a takes -o: mama → mamo.
Full names in -a take -o: Anno. Formal or neutral in tone.
A soft-stem diminutive takes -u: Aniu. This is the warm everyday form.
A full name, so -o, even though the stem ends in hardened sz: Agnieszko.
Hard d, no diminutive suffix → -o: Magdo.
l behaves as soft in pet names: Olu.
Consonant-final feminine → -y after hardened c: nocy. Same as the locative, w nocy.
krew → krwi, with the e dropping. The same form serves the locative and genitive.
wieś → wsi, with the e dropping and ś → s.
-a → -o: Warszawo. Cities are addressed like people.
Polsko! — the anthem line. Polsku would be the locative, w Polsku? no: w Polsce.
A noun in -a always takes -o: ulico. The -y ending belongs only to consonant-final nouns.
Again -o: różo. Róży is the genitive and dative.
Feminine nouns in -i never change: pani.

sets.title: -e, -u or -o?
sets.ask: Which ending does the vocative take?

items.why: Hard t → -e, with t → ci: kocie.
k, g and ch take -u: Marku.
l takes -u: królu. Only ł goes to -e, as in Michale.
Hard n → -e, with n → ni: panie.
Feminine nouns in -i are unchanged: pani.
There is no separate vocative plural: studenci.
Boże — an irregular -e where you would expect -u.

sets.title: Type the vocative — nouns
sets.ask: Type the vocative (the word alone, no exclamation mark).

items.why: s → si and a → e: lesie. Same as the locative.
s → si and a → e: czasie.
domu, the same as the locative w domu.
synu — the old u-stem, matching o synu.
ą → ę and ż takes -u: mężu.
ń takes -u and the e drops: uczniu.
An ordinary noun in -a keeps -o even on a soft stem: ziemio.

sets.title: Type the vocative — names
sets.ask: Type the vocative of the name.

items.why: Marku — k takes -u, the e drops.
Pawle — ł → l, and the e drops.
Adamie — here d stays d. Compare Dawidzie.
Dawidzie — here d → dzi. These two have to be learned.
Maćku — the ć is already there; -ek → -ku.
Olu — l behaves as soft in pet names.

items.q: You are speaking to your doctor, a man.
items.why: Masculine titles take the vocative: panie doktorze. The ending also marks that the doctor is a man.

items.q: You are speaking to your doctor, a woman.
items.why: Feminine titles of profession are indeclinable, so the form stays pani doktor.

items.q: You are speaking to your professor, a man.
You are speaking to your professor, a woman.
You are speaking to your boss, a man (prezes).
You want a stranger’s attention in the street.
items.why: A fixed expression with the accusative. The vocative panie is not used after przepraszam.

items.q: You want to ask a stranger for help politely.
items.why: Another fixed accusative phrase: proszę pana.

items.q: You greet a customer as a shop assistant.
items.why: The dative — good day to you. It looks like a vocative but is not one.

items.q: You address a group of mixed men and women.
items.why: Państwo covers a mixed group. It is already plural, so it does not change.
Both words are in the vocative: księże (irregular) and proboszczu.
siostra → siostro, the ordinary feminine -a rule.

items.q: You call to a monk, warmly.
You want to say “O my God!”
items.why: Boże is the irregular vocative; mój does not change.

items.q: You address a man whose surname is Nowak.
items.why: PWN: surnames have a vocative equal to the nominative. (Nowaku exists traditionally but is marked.)

items.q: You address a woman whose surname is Kowalska.
items.why: Unchanged — and Kowalsko is the classic error PWN warns about.

items.q: You write an email opening to a man you know, Marek.
items.why: Both pan and the name go into the vocative.

items.q: You write to a woman you know, Anna.
items.why: Formal letters use the full name in -o, not the diminutive.

items.q: You greet a friend, Kasia, in a message.
items.why: The diminutive in -u is the warm everyday form.

items.q: A formal letter to Marek opens with…
items.why: In writing the vocative is obligatory. The nominative here is an error, not a style.

items.q: You shout to a friend across the street.
items.why: Both are heard, but Marku is the traditional and always-correct form. Marek is the modern colloquial drift.
Titles keep the vocative most stubbornly, because the ending signals the gender.
After the pronoun ty the vocative is unavoidable.
Family terms are never left in the nominative when addressed.

items.q: You call your colleague Krzysztof in the office.
items.why: The traditional form. The nominative is spreading, but the vocative is never wrong.

items.q: A newspaper headline addresses the readers.
items.why: Plural — and the plural vocative equals the nominative.

items.q: You address a woman you do not know, in a shop.
items.why: pani ends in -i and never changes.

items.q: You speak to a judge in court.
items.why: The fixed formula uses sąd, not sędzia: Wysoki Sądzie.

items.q: You address a group of students.
items.why: Plural vocative = nominative. There is no plural ending.

items.q: You write a card to your grandmother.
items.why: babcia → babciu; the adjective stays kochana.

items.q: You address God in a prayer.
items.why: The irregular vocative Boże; Bogu is dative or locative.

items.q: You address a police officer, a man.
items.why: A colloquial set phrase: władza → władzo, masculine in -a.

items.q: You address your teacher, a woman.
You address your teacher, a man.
You address the reader of a manual, one person, formally.
items.why: czytelnik → czytelniku, the ordinary masculine -u after k.

sets.title: In the sentence
sets.ask: Complete the sentence with the right form.

items.why: Marku — the address, set off by the comma.
This one is not the vocative: przepraszam takes the accusative, pana.

items.hint: a doctor, a man, called Marek
items.why: Panie doktorze — the title takes the vocative, and the name Marku follows it. In practice Poles would just say Panie Marku.
Sąsiedzie — d → dzi and ą → ę.
Each address takes its own vocative: Aniu i Marku.
Boże mój! — vocative plus unchanged mój.
Warszawo — places are addressed like people.
Panie — from Pan, used for God and for a gentleman alike.
Boże is the irregular vocative of Bóg.
Matko — feminine -a → -o. Matka Boska is the nominative, used when talking about her.
Masculine in -a → -o, and the vocative is compulsory after ty.
Jezu is the fixed exclamatory form. Jezusie also exists, but O Jezu! is the idiom.
Chryste — the old vocative, kept in exclamations.
duch → duchu; the adjective święty stays.
przyjaciel → przyjacielu; mój and drogi stay unchanged.
Plural vocative = nominative, and drodzy agrees with the masculine-personal plural.

items.q: “Sir!” — calling a man in the street
items.why: pan → panie. Pan! alone sounds like a bark.
